title: KV reuse decay and bandwidth noise experiments
body:
Summary:

This note collects a set of small experiments exploring how short-term reuse decay and background memory-bandwidth noise interact to create apparent KV cache instability (spurious evictions, increased p99 tail). Goal is to (1) measure reuse decay constants in production-like traces, (2) reproduce p99 spikes with synthetic noise, and (3) validate a low-cost mitigation (batch-coalescing + gentle TTL bump).

Why this matters (quick):
- Customers observe occasional latency tails even when aggregate occupancy looks healthy.
- Hypothesis: transient reuse decay + background DMA/peer traffic increases read latency, causing delayed KV warming and more frequent eviction churn.
- If true, mitigation may be cheaper than increasing reserved capacity.

High-level plan:
- Experiment A: Estimate reuse decay (probability a key is requested again after t ms) from request traces (sampled prod traces + replay).
- Experiment B: Microbench memory bandwidth interference using fio + synthetic KV probe workload on a dev rig to see p50/p95/p99 latency shift under varying BW noise patterns.
- Experiment C: End-to-end replay with TTL bump strategy (increase keep-alive window by 1.5x for recently accessed keys) and batch-coalescing to amortize stalls.

Notes on environment and constraints:
- Hardware used: 2x A100-40GB (NVLink peer enabled), Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 11.8 stack.
- Runtime: local dev cluster (k8s kind) mimicking single serving node: runtime binary built from pr 387.
- Traces: sampled user_session traces from Jan 2025 (redacted), replay tool uses same seq length distribution as production.
- Measurement tools: perf, nvprof (older but useful), nvidia-smi dmon for GPU memory traffic, sar/iostat for host bandwidth, and custom KV latency histogram exporter.

Experiment A: Reuse decay estimation
- Method:
  1) From sampled traces (N=2.1M requests), tag KV keys by token-prefix fingerprint.
  2) For each key, collect inter-arrival times between successive accesses.
  3) Build survival curve S(t) = P(inter-arrival > t). Compute hazard and fit simple exponential and Weibull models.
- Findings (quick):
  - Short-term reuse dominant: ~62% of reuses happen within 150ms, 82% within 500ms.
  - Tail: a long but thin tail; Weibull shape k~0.7 fits better than exponential (implies heavier tail).
  - Effective decay constant (exponential fit) lambda ~ 0.006/ms (i.e., half-life ~115ms).
- Implication: small shifts in read latency distribution around 50-200ms timescales can have outsized effect on cache hit probability for hot short-lived keys.

Experiment B: BW noise microbench
- Setup:
  - Baseline: KV probe workload (single-threaded client issuing point reads, QPS tuned to mimic realistic concurrency); measure KV read latency histogram.
  - Noise generator: fio sequential read load pinned to different NUMA nodes, plus small bursts of memcpy patterns to stress DMA engine.
- Observations:
  - Baseline p99 ~ 12.2ms, p50 ~ 1.8ms.
  - With continuous fio seq-read at ~8 GB/s on same host, p99 jumps to 28ms, p50 unaffected (~2.0ms).
  - With intermittent burst noise (200ms bursts every 1s) p99 shows spiky behavior aligned with bursts, often exceeding 50ms for short windows.
  - NVLink dmon counters show increased peer-memory traffic correlated with p99 spikes; CPU side iostat shows increased read latencies as well.
- Quick interpretation: KV-serving read path is sensitive to host memory bandwidth contention and peer-DMA bursts; these raise tail latency without shifting median significantly.

Experiment C: Replay + mitigation test
- Baseline replay: full session replay with default eviction/TTL. Measured artifacts:
  - Hit ratio: 91.6% steady-state, but transient dips to 84% coincident with BW bursts.
  - Request p99 tails (end-to-end) plunged during dips: baseline p99 52ms, dips reached 110-180ms.
- Mitigation tried:
  1) Soft TTL bump: when a key is accessed, record recent access timestamp; on eviction, prefer to retain keys accessed within last T_bump ms. Implemented as a probabilistic TTL extension (exponential backoff decay). T_bump chosen ~200ms (roughly 1.7x observed half-life).
  2) Batch-coalescing: group simultaneous small reads for the same key fingerprint in a worker queue for up to 5ms to allow cache affinity to be exploited and reduce simultaneous cache thrashing.
- Results:
  - Soft TTL bump alone: hit ratio improved during bursts (min dip now 88%), p99 during bursts reduced by ~35% on average (e.g., from 140ms -> 92ms in one run).
  - Batch-coalescing alone: reduced peak QPS on backend and smoothed p99 spikes by ~20%, but increased tail of single-request latency slightly due to queuing (median unaffected).
  - Combined: most robust—min dip 90.5% hit ratio, p99 spikes reduced by ~50% compared to baseline worst-case. Overall p95 improved modestly.
- Cost/side-effects:
  - Soft TTL bump increases steady-state resident set slightly (~4-6% memory overhead in these runs).
  - Batch-coalescing tuning is sensitive: too long coalescing window increases median latency for strict SLOs; 3-6ms looked like a good sweet spot for our workload.

Profiling artifacts and commands (notes to self):
- perf script + flamegraphs for slow samples: `perf record -F 99 -a -g -- ./runtime --kv-probe` then `perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded`
- nvtx regions inserted in runtime to correlate host stalls with kernel launches. NVTX traces looked noisy during fio bursts.
- iostat -x 1 to correlate host disk/bandwidth stalls (we saw read await increase during worst bursts).
- dmesg and OOM checks were clean (no swapping).

Open questions / next actions:
- Validate on a multi-tenant node where other GPU workloads generate NVLink traffic (we only tested host-level BW here).
- Measure interaction with quantized model kernels: quantized kernels lower compute but increase memory IO; hypothesis: they could be more sensitive to BW noise.
- Consider a lightweight admission policy: if detected global BW spike, temporarily increase TTL bump aggressiveness cluster-wide via soft signal. Need to prototype signal path in control-plane.
- Follow up PR to add metrics: per-key recent-access histogram and an eviction-churn counter to production exporter. Jira: GHD-1123 (linked).

Quick TODOs:
- [ ] Run Experiment B on staging with multi-tenant GPU workloads (assign to Ethan).
- [ ] Add per-key recent-access histogram metric to runtime (Maya).
- [ ] Prototype global BW spike signal in control-plane and simple TTL modulation (Priya, Liam).

Closing note:
This feels promising: small, cheap TTL nudges plus micro-batching seem to cut the worst of the tails without large memory or complexity costs. The risk is over-retaining cold keys; instrumentation will be critical to ensure memory overhead stays bounded.

Appendix (raw numbers from one representative run):
- Baseline replay (no mitigation): hit_ratio_avg=0.916, hit_ratio_min_dip=0.84, p50=2.1ms, p95=18.6ms, p99=52.3ms, worst_p99_during_burst=178.4ms
- Soft TTL bump: hit_ratio_avg=0.924, hit_ratio_min_dip=0.88, p50=2.2ms, p95=16.1ms, p99=35.4ms, worst_p99_during_burst=102.9ms, memory_overhead=+5%
- Batch-coalescing (3ms window): hit_ratio_avg=0.919, hit_ratio_min_dip=0.86, p50=2.6ms, p95=15.3ms, p99=41.5ms
- Combined: hit_ratio_avg=0.931, hit_ratio_min_dip=0.905, p50=2.5ms, p95=12.8ms, p99=26.1ms

If this aligns with folks' intuitions I'll continue: more runs, better statistical significance, add per-key retention telemetry and a cheap feedback signal to limit memory growth.

-- Priya
(researching small, deployable fixes for KV churn)
